# Deep Dive Two: The Scaling Era

The last decade of artificial intelligence developments was largely inspired by scaling laws, first described by Jared Kaplan and later refined by Jordan Hoffmann, which suggest that the performance of an AI model will improve by a predictable amount with a given increase in computational resources and training data size. 227 

These are not laws of nature (like the law of universal gravitation); rather they are experimentally observed patterns (like Moore’s Law, which states that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles roughly every two years). Like Moore’s Law, the AI scaling regularities are remarkably robust: you can accurately predict the performance of a model with a thousand parameters as well as one with a trillion. The difference is the speed: AI models’ capabilities have been doubling every three to six months, not every two years. In the words of deep learning pioneer Ilya Sutskever: “If you mix some compute with some data into a neural net of a certain size, you will get results, and you will know that it will be better if you just scale the recipe up. [...] Companies love this because it gives you a very low-risk way of investing your resources.” This observation characterizes the scaling era in AI.

However, more recent empirical work suggests that the predictive power of scaling laws may be more limited than initially assumed. While early studies demonstrated smooth improvements with scale, 228 subsequent analyses show that downstream performance and real-world capabilities often exhibit irregular, domain-dependent scaling behavior. 229 In some cases, smaller, more efficiently trained models outperform significantly larger systems, indicating that scale alone is not a reliable predictor of capability. 230 These developments suggest that the relationship between compute and performance is becoming increasingly complex, with gains now often driven by improvements in data quality, training procedures, model architecture, and inference-time compute rather than model size alone.

As a result, the scaling paradigm is increasingly complemented—and in some cases challenged—by approaches that emphasize sample efficiency and computational efficiency rather than sheer size. Advances such as improved data curation, model distillation, instruction tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation have demonstrated substantial performance gains without proportional increases in compute. 231 

It is not clear when the scaling era will end, or if it already is ending. Despite the release of ever-larger models, we have seen several smaller models rise to near the top of leaderboards. 232 Another quote from Sutskever implies that research may be more important than just scaling today: “ Scaling the pre-training is essentially tapped out. If you just multiply the scale by 100x now, you won’t get a qualitative change in capability.”

## The Race to Scale: Compute

The race to scale has had a number of important consequences.

First, the extreme compute resources required to build such models began to dramatically limit the number of organizations capable of developing frontier AI models. According to Epoch AI, the computing power used to train frontier language models has grown roughly fivefold per year since 2020, and the largest known AI data center now has the capacity of more than a million of Nvidia’s H100 specialized AI chips (GPUs). The capital cost of acquiring such computing infrastructure would place it beyond the reach of all but the very wealthiest international universities, while the associated energy costs alone would dwarf the budgets of most academic research projects. As a result, the development of very large, state-of-the-art models became increasingly concentrated within a small number of companies worldwide, most notably the major Silicon Valley technology firms (see also discussion in SQ8). In turn, this has meant that the development of leading AI models increasingly occurs behind closed doors.

This concentration reflects a broader structural dynamic in which access to large-scale compute becomes a prerequisite for participation in frontier research, with breakthroughs increasingly clustered in well-capitalized organizations and regions. 233 The fact that general-purpose AI would in effect largely be owned by a small number of U.S.-based private companies prompted a number of nation-states to begin considering the possibility of sovereign AI capabilities, for example, investing in national and international schemes to develop independent AI infrastructure and GPT-class AI systems. In the U.S., shortly after his second-term inauguration, President Donald J. Trump announced an initiative called Stargate, aimed at developing a $500 billion strategic compute resource for U.S. AI.

A second major consequence of the race to scale was the dramatic increase in demand for both the semiconductors required to train these models and the data on which they depend. We examined the geopolitical implications in Deep Dive One: Supply Chains and Environmental Impact; here, it is sufficient to note that this demand led to an extraordinary increase in the valuations of leading AI chip manufacturers, most notably Nvidia, the company that pioneered the development of GPUs. In October 2025, Nvidia reached a market capitalization of $5 trillion, the largest of any company in the world, arguably making it the most valuable company in human history. This valuation exceeded the GDP of almost every nation on Earth. This extraordinary growth was driven purely by the demand for the semiconductors that are developed by Nvidia, which are the chip of choice for training AI models.

More generally, the race to scale prompted vast investment in data centers: estimates suggest that if current demand continues then a further $6.7 trillion capital investment in data centers will be required. Many serious commentators suggest that this enormous capital investment, coupled with spend on semiconductors and ancillary hardware, is actually propping up the U.S. economy, possibly even preventing it from going into recession. The European AI Strategy builds upon the concept of cross-national centralized AI Gigafactories—massive, gigawatt-level data centers with up to 100,000 advanced AI processors designed to enable next-generation models.

The economic justification for these investments relies on the assumption of sustained returns to scale. Yet studies suggest that the marginal gains from additional compute may be decreasing over time. 234 If so, the long-term sustainability of continued exponential investment in infrastructure may be uncertain.

There has been considerable pushback about the scale of data center development, on a number of grounds. First, data centers in 2026 are physically enormous facilities; they are noisy and tend not to be aesthetically pleasing. It is therefore understandable that people living in the vicinity of a new data center development would resent the imposition of such facilities in their neighborhood. Some people protest the impact that large companies and technologies have on our society, and these protests have even led to violence. The environmental impact of data centers (energy, water, CO2) is an important issue that we cover in Deep Dive One: Supply Chains and Environmental Impact. Data centers do provide some jobs, but only about one-tenth the number provided by a similarly sized traditional manufacturing facility.

The financial model underpinning data center development on the current scale has come into question. The argument for building data centers is that the new technology requires it, and that the up-front cost will later be recouped by the benefits gained. An analogy is often made with the development of railroads in the 19th century. Laying down railroads was enormously costly at the time, but the basic infrastructure had a long timeline: railroad tracks themselves are typically good for decades, and the infrastructure to support them can have a lifetime measured in centuries. By contrast, the computers that populate data centers often get replaced after several years as newer technologies become available. Thus not only is the current investment in data centers enormous but it has a very short window in which to show returns.

Finally, the extraordinary scale of current investment in AI infrastructure has raised serious questions about economic sustainability. Much of this investment has been financed through borrowing and external capital, including pension funds and private equity, rather than solely through retained earnings of technology firms. Despite the bullish claims of big tech companies, it is far from clear whether anticipated returns justify this level of expenditure, especially as models are often improved by training new versions rather than refining existing ones. In short, the scale of investment in data centers risks a market crash unless markets remain convinced that investments will be recouped.

## The Race to Scale: Data

The race to scale also triggered an intense scramble for training data. Crucially, compute-optimal training regimes (for example, Chinchilla) show that the training data required for a model must scale proportionally with model size: larger models require comparably larger training datasets in order to show improvements. And large language models are particularly data-hungry. Although precise figures for more recent models are not publicly available, OpenAI disclosed that GPT-3 was trained on approximately 45 terabytes of textual data. At this scale, the World Wide Web provides the only realistic source of such volumes of text, and it quickly became standard practice to scrape text from virtually every available online resource. These resources included online public data sources such as Wikipedia, social media sources such as Twitter, and discussion forums such as Reddit, as well as commercial and governmental websites.

The widespread use of data sources like the World Wide Web provoked significant concerns about copyright. If an LLM has effectively ingested substantial portions of the World Wide Web, it has necessarily absorbed vast quantities of copyrighted material. Unsurprisingly, this led to widespread objections from rights holders and, ultimately, to a growing number of legal challenges in multiple jurisdictions. AI model providers argued that the use of these data sources in training AI models did not represent a copyright infringement since, firstly, LLMs do not store copyrighted works in any conventional sense (one cannot in general point to any specific part of an LLM’s neural networks and say, “That’s where my data is stored”), and, secondly, LLMs are not derivative works in the sense of copyright law. Copyright law was simply not designed with AI models and neural networks in mind.

There are several open lawsuits, such as the one where the New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft over their use of copyrighted work. We cannot judge at this point how the many lawsuits underway will pan out; nor can we predict what the legal landscape around data, copyright, and AI models will ultimately look like. Summer 2025 court decisions in the U.S. have suggested AI use of copyrighted material for training is fair use, including cases against Meta and Anthropic. At the same time, Anthropic was found to have used books in training without paying for them and eventually settled the lawsuit related to the pirated books with a $1.5 billion payout. This is the largest copyright settlement in legal history (by some considerable distance).
